bibl.title: The Anatomy of the Facebook Social Graph

person.p: the tag layer; a sentence written by the tagger about the paper, always anchored to a quotation but not itself a quotation

span.label: existence
span.quote: First, we characterize the global structure of the graph, determining that the social network is nearly fully connected, with 99.91% of individuals belonging to a single large connected component, and we confirm the ‘six degrees of separation’ phenomenon on a global scale.

span.label: structure of the Facebook social graph
span.quote: In this work, we characterize the structure of the world’s largest online social network, Facebook, in an effort to advance the state of the art in the empirical study of social networks.

span.label: large-scale-network-analysis
span.quote: Unless otherwise noted, calculations were performed on a Hadoop cluster with 2,250 machines, using the Hadoop/Hive data analysis framework developed at Facebook [45, 46].

span.label: The paper's own definition of an 'active' user departs from Facebook's, so its statistics differ from company figures.
span.quote: We note that this definition is not precisely Facebook’s ordinary definition of active user, and therefore some of our statistics differ slightly from company statistics.

span.label: Country assignment relies on geo-IP data, which is imperfect and only reliable at national granularity.
span.quote: While imperfect, so-called geo-IP data is generally reliable on a national level.

span.label: The analysis is acknowledged as non-exhaustive with respect to available network measures.
span.quote: While our computations have elucidated many aspects of the structure of the world’s largest social network, we have certainly not exhausted the possibilities of network analysis.

span.label: The 'six degrees' confirmation is a statement about percentages of pairs in a friendship graph, not a repeat of the experiment that produced the phrase.
span.quote: As Figure 2 shows, fully 92% of all pairs of Facebook users were within five degrees of separation, and 99.6% were within six degrees

span.label: The object studied is an abstraction the authors themselves call limited.
span.quote: This abstract view of human relationships, while certainly limited, has been very useful for characterizing social relationships

span.label: A small group of accounts sits far outside the typical user, so the average describes nobody in particular.
span.quote: The small population of users with abnormally high degrees, sometimes called hubs in the networks literature, have degrees far larger than the average or median Facebook user

span.label: 'active user' - STIPULATED, AND EXPLICITLY NOT THE PLATFORM'S: logged in within 28 days and holding at least one friend, which the authors state is not Facebook's ordinary definition and is why their statistics differ from the company's; the 721 million figure counts exactly what this sentence picks out
span.quote: We defined a user of Facebook as an active member of the social network if they logged into the site in the last 28 days from our time of measurement in May 2011 and had at least one Facebook friend. We note that this definition is not precisely Facebook’s ordinary definition of active user, and therefore some of our statistics differ slightly from company statistics

span.label: 'six degrees of separation' - MILGRAM'S PHRASE ON A DIFFERENT INSTRUMENT: the original is letter-forwarding chains among Americans, this is shortest paths in a friendship graph, and the paper says the phenomenon is here SEEN in Facebook rather than claiming the two measurements are the same
span.quote: Short path lengths between individuals, the so-called “six degrees of separation” found by Stanley Milgram’s experiments investigating the social network of the United States [26], are here seen in Facebook on a global scale

span.label: the local clustering coefficient - READ AS A PERCENTAGE OF FRIEND PAIRS: an average coefficient of 0.14 for users with 100 friends is glossed as 14% of a median user's friend pairs being friends themselves, so an average over users is reported as a fact about a median one
span.quote: for users with 100 friends, the average local clustering coefficient is 0.14, indicating that for a median user, 14% of all their friend pairs are themselves friends

span.label: replicates → the small-world / six-degrees-of-separation phenomenon (Milgram)
span.quote: the average distance between pairs of users was 4

span.label: replicates → Stanley Milgram's 'six degrees of separation' experiments [26]
span.quote: Short path lengths between individuals, the so-called “six degrees of separation” found by Stanley Milgram’s experiments investigating the social network of the United States [26], are here seen in Facebook on a global scale.

span.label: extends → Feld's friendship paradox ('your friends have more friends than you') [30]
span.quote: This phenomena has been discussed at length by Feld [30], and Facebook displays the effect on a grand scale.

span.label: builds-on → Watts and Strogatz's small-world networks [44]
span.quote: Many other empirical networks, social and non-social, have also been observed with these characteristics, and Watts and Strogatz called networks with these properties ‘smallworld networks’ [44].

span.label: short path lengths —same-as→ degrees of separation
span.quote: Short path lengths between individuals, the so-called “six degrees of separation” found by Stanley Milgram’s experiments investigating the social network of the United States [26], are here seen in Facebook on a global scale

span.label: active user —contrasted-with→ hubs
span.quote: The small population of users with abnormally high degrees, sometimes called hubs in the networks literature, have degrees far larger than the average or median Facebook user

span.label: 721 million — size of the Facebook graph analysed (May 2011)
span.quote: a network then comprised of 721 million active users. To our knowledge, this is the largest social network ever analyzed.

span.label: 99.91% — fraction of users in the single large connected component
span.quote: the social network is nearly fully connected, with 99.91% of individuals belonging to a single large connected component

span.label: 4.7 — average distance between Facebook users (May 2011) — four degrees
span.quote: The average distance between users on Facebook in May 2011 was 4.7

span.label: Although the graph is globally sparse, users local neighborhoods are surprisingly dense, and the graph shows clear assortativity by demographic and network properties.
span.quote: while the Facebook graph as a whole is clearly sparse, the graph neighborhoods of users contain surprisingly dense structure

span.label: user degree / neighborhood locality
span.quote: the average local clustering coefficient and degeneracy of graph neighborhoods

span.label: global connectivity / average path length / assortativity
span.term: global connectivity / average path length / assortativity
span.quote: The average distance between users on Facebook in May 2011 was 4.7

span.label: assortativity
span.quote: we characterize the assortativity patterns present in the graph by studying the basic demographic and network properties of users

span.label: connected component
span.quote: 99.91% of individuals belonging to a single large connected component

span.label: correlation
span.quote: For the Facebook network, r = 0.226, displaying positive correlations with similar magnitude to other social graphs.

span.label: sample-size
span.quote: According to our definition of active, the population of active Facebook users consisted of around n = 721 million individuals at the time of our measurements.

span.label: statistical-significance
span.quote: Restricting the comparison to individuals age 13 or more and with access to the internet (the set of individuals eligible to have Facebook accounts) would put this percentage significantly higher.

p.note: The full text of this article is not redistributable, so it is not included here. Every tag above carries the exact sentence it was made from, quoted under fair quotation. The article itself is at https://arxiv.org/abs/1111.4503.
